rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance annual allowable rent increase
rules.requirement:
For rent-controlled units, rent may rise each year by no more than the annual allowable increase published by the Rent Board.
- March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027: 1.6%. To get the dollar amount, multiply base rent by .016 (e.g. $2,000.00 x .016 = $32.00, so new base rent is $2,032.00).
- March 1, 2025 – February 28, 2026: 1.4%.
- March 1, 2024 – February 28, 2025: 1.7%.

Exempt from the rent increase limits (but still subject to the Ordinance's just-cause eviction rules):
- Newly constructed units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979.
- Tenancies eligible for a rent increase under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act.
- Some tenancies where rent is regulated by another government agency.

For capital improvement petitions, the Rent Board publishes imputed interest rates for petitions filed March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027:
- 4.1% for 7-year amortization.
- 4.3% for 10-year amortization.
- 4.6% for 15-year amortization.
- 4.8% for 20-year amortization.

The uncompensated labor rate is $40.40 for work starting 6/29/26 or later.
rules.key_value: 1.6% annual allowable increase for 3/1/2026–2/28/2027 (base rent x .016); 1.4% for 2025-26; 1.7% for 2024-25

coverage.summary: Rent-controlled units under the San Francisco Rent Ordinance. Units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979 are exempt from the increase limits, as are Costa-Hawkins-eligible tenancies and some agency-regulated tenancies.
coverage.other_conditions: Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12 exempts housing under a stricter local rent control. The 1.6% local cap is below the state formula, so the local rule governs for covered units.

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just cause eviction and relocation payments (§§ 37.9(a), 37.9A, 37.9C)
rules.requirement:
A landlord may evict a tenant from a unit covered by the Rent Ordinance only for one of 17 just causes under § 37.9(a), and that cause must be the dominant motive. Expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership is not just cause.

The causes are:
- Non-payment, habitual late payment or frequent bounced checks.
- Failure to cure a substantial breach.
- Severe, continuing or recurring nuisance.
- Illegal use. This excludes mere occupancy of an unwarranted unit and a single short-term rental violation cured within 30 days.
- Refusal to sign a like extension or renewal.
- Refusal of lawful access.
- An unapproved subtenant being the only occupant at the end of the term.
- Owner or (limited) relative move-in.
- Approved condominium conversion sale.
- Demolition or permanent removal from housing use.
- Temporary capital improvement or rehabilitation work, with immediate reoccupancy.
- Substantial rehabilitation of a building at least 50 years old and essentially uninhabitable, costing at least 75% of new construction.
- Ellis Act withdrawal of all units.
- Lead remediation required by Health Code Articles 11 or 26.
- Demolition or removal under a Chapter 56 development agreement.
- Expired Good Samaritan occupancy agreement, with notice served within 60 days.
- Demolition for a development project under Planning Code § 317.

Just cause is also required to remove housing services such as parking, storage and laundry. Under § 37.2(r), services may be removed temporarily for mandatory soft-story seismic retrofit work.

Relocation payments (§ 37.9C) apply to evictions for owner/relative move-in, demolition or permanent removal, temporary capital improvement work, or substantial rehabilitation. For notices served 3/1/26–2/28/27:
- $8,245 per tenant.
- Maximum $24,733 per unit.
- Plus $5,497 for each elderly (60+) or disabled tenant or household with minor children.
Temporary capital improvement evictions under 20 days are governed instead by Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.9.

Ellis Act relocation payments (§ 37.9A), for notices served 3/1/26–2/28/27:
- $11,110.05 per tenant.
- Maximum $33,330.13 per unit.
- Plus $7,443.90 for each elderly (62+) or disabled tenant.

Relocation amounts are fixed by the date the eviction notice is served and reset each March 1.
rules.key_value: 17 just causes (dominant motive required). Relocation for notices served 3/1/2026–2/28/2027: § 37.9C $8,245/tenant, max $24,733/unit, +$5,497 per elderly (60+)/disabled tenant or household with minor children; Ellis Act (§ 37.9A) $11,110.05/tenant, max $33,330.13/unit, +$7,443.90 per elderly (62+)/disabled tenant. Prior period: $8,062/$24,184/$5,375 and $10,863.45/$32,590.33/$7,278.67.

coverage.summary: Rental units covered by the San Francisco Rent Ordinance. This includes tenancies exempt from the rent increase limits: units first obtaining a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, Costa-Hawkins-eligible tenancies, and some agency-regulated tenancies.
coverage.other_conditions: Just-cause protection reaches units on both sides of the June 13, 1979 rent-control cutoff, so no construction cutoff applies. Under Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2(i), a qualifying local just-cause ordinance applies instead of the state rule.

rules.exemptions: Relocation for temporary capital improvement evictions of less than 20 days is governed by Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.9, not § 37.9C.
rules.effective_date_note: The documents do not state when the Ordinance or §§ 37.9, 37.9A or 37.9C took effect. The § 37.9C rate archive begins with notices served 8/10/06 and the Ellis Act archive with 3/01/06. Current relocation amounts apply to notices served 3/1/2026–2/28/2027 and reset each March 1.
rules.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction.
rules.review_note: The § 37.9A attribution of Ellis Act relocation rests only on the Rent Board's '578 Multilingual Relocation Payments 37.9A' link label. The overview gives no notice content or timing beyond the Good Samaritan 60-day rule. supersedes_state_rule assumes the Ordinance qualifies under Civ. Code § 1946.2(i) (adopted on or before Sept. 1, 2019, or more protective with a binding finding). The documents do not state its adoption date, although the June 13, 1979 cutoff suggests it is long-standing.
rules.source_notes: Merged the § 37.9(a) overview (D079) with the § 37.9C and § 37.9A relocation rates from the Rent Board archive (D082) and current rates page (D083). The current-period amounts agree across both rate pages. All are parts of the same Rent Ordinance eviction section family.

rules.title: San Francisco annual security deposit interest rate
rules.requirement:
The Rent Board publishes an annual interest rate on tenant security deposits:
- 4.2% for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027.
- 5.0% for 2025-26.
- 5.2% for 2024-25.

The page does not state who must pay the interest, which units are covered, or how it is credited. Deposit caps and return rules come from state law (Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5).
rules.key_value: 4.2% security deposit interest for 3/1/2026–2/28/2027 (5.0% for 2025-26; 5.2% for 2024-25)

coverage.summary: Coverage is not stated in the documents; only the annual rate is published.
coverage.other_conditions: Complementary to the state deposit cap and return rules in Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5.

rules.effective_date_note: The 4.2% rate applies March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027 and is reset annually. The documents do not state when the underlying interest requirement took effect.

rules.title: San Francisco ban on algorithmic rent-setting devices (Rent Ordinance § 37.10C)
rules.requirement:
The law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco. An 'algorithmic device' is a device, such as a software program, that uses algorithms to analyze nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend to a landlord what rent to charge for a vacant unit.

A tenant or the City Attorney may bring a civil action. Per a secondary source:
- Tenants may seek damages, injunctive relief and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.
- Each month of use for each affected unit may be a separate violation.
rules.key_value: Ban on sale or use of algorithmic rent-setting devices using nonpublic competitor data; civil action by tenant or City Attorney; per secondary source, civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation, each unit-month potentially separate; effective Oct. 14, 2024

coverage.summary: Residential units in San Francisco, and sellers and users of qualifying algorithmic devices. The documents state no building or landlord-size limits.
coverage.other_conditions: Operates alongside the state Cartwright Act common pricing algorithm prohibition (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729).

rules.effective_date_note: Per the Rent Board notice of October 16, 2024. The enactment date is not stated.
rules.quoted_span: adding Section 37.10C to the Rent Ordinance went into effect on October 14, 2024. The law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco.
rules.review_note: The ordinance text is not captured. The penalty amounts and unit-month exposure come from a secondary law-firm alert citing § 37.10C(b) and (d). The ordinance is at issue in Gomez v. Greystar Management Services LLC (N.D. Cal.). The documents do not address how it interacts with state AB 325.
rules.source_notes: Official Rent Board notice (D081). The Morgan Lewis alert of Aug. 21, 2026 (DX06) gives 'effective October 2024' (month only), which is consistent with Oct. 14, 2024.

also_supported_by.quoted_span: The term “algorithmic device” means a device such as a software program that uses algorithms to analyze nonpublic competitor rental data for the purposes of providing a landlord recommendations on what rent to charge for a vacant unit.
Each month of use for each affected dwelling unit may constitute a separate violation, and tenants may seek damages, injunctive relief, and civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation.
